description:
Photinia Red Leaf (Photinia spp.) is a decorative shrub known for its bright red new leaves. It is mildly toxic to cats and not safe for them to chew. The plant contains chemicals called cyanogenic glycosides, especially in its young red leaves and seeds.

When a cat chews and digests the leaves or seeds, these chemicals break down and release cyanide. Cyanide stops cells from using oxygen properly. Fortunately, the amount of these chemicals in the plant is usually low. A cat would need to eat a large amount to get seriously sick.

If your cat eats a small amount, you might see drooling, vomiting, or low energy. Eating larger amounts could cause breathing problems and weakness. Because the red leaves might look interesting to outdoor cats, it is best to keep them away. Please contact a veterinarian if your cat eats a noticeable amount of this plant.
emergencyNote: Antidote Therapy (Sodium Nitrite and Sodium Thiosulfate, OR Hydroxycobalamin)
name: Photina Red Leaf
safetyNotes: Toxic compounds: cyanogenic glycosides (nandinin / p-glucosyloxymandelonitrile); young red leaves contain higher concentrations than mature green leaves
Mechanism: the cyanogenic glycoside releases HCN via beta-glucosidase, inhibiting cellular respiration at high doses
Symptoms: drooling, vomiting, lethargy with minor ingestion; heavy ingestion may cause laboured breathing and weakness
The attractive red foliage may make this shrub appealing to cats outdoors
Contact your vet if your cat ingests a significant amount of leaves

symptoms.name: Vomiting, diarrhea, and excessive drooling
symptoms.notes: While vomiting and drooling are common early signs of many plant poisonings, the presence of an almond-like odor on the breath is a specific and classic indicator of cyanide gas release. 2. Respiratory Distress

symptoms.name: Tachypnea (rapid breathing), severe respiratory distress, panting, and gasping for breath
symptoms.notes: This is a direct result of tissue hypoxia. The cyanide prevents the cat's cells from utilizing oxygen, causing the respiratory system to go into overdrive in a futile attempt to oxygenate the body. 3. Mucous Membrane Discoloration and Cardiovascular Shock

symptoms.name: Unusually bright red or pink gums (brick red mucous membranes), hypotension (low blood pressure), and cardiac arrhythmias
symptoms.notes: A classic sign of cyanide toxicosis is cherry-red blood coloring2. Because the cells cannot absorb oxygen from the blood, the oxygen remains trapped in the bloodstream, turning the cat's gums an unusual, bright cherry or brick red23. symptoms.name: Dilated pupils, sudden collapse, muscle seizures, convulsions, coma, and death
symptoms.notes: The brain is highly sensitive to oxygen deprivation. As cellular energy production halts, neurological collapse can occur after large ingestions. Death is possible in severe cyanide toxicosis but is rare in pets.

One method uses sodium nitrite to combine with cyanide and form cyanomethemoglobin, followed by sodium thiosulfate to convert it into water-soluble thiocyanate, which the cat can safely excrete in its urine1. treatments.description: To prevent the plant material from further breaking down and releasing cyanide into the bloodstream, the veterinarian will medically induce vomiting to empty the stomach. This is followed by administering a dose of activated charcoal combined with a cathartic to bind and pass any remaining toxins out of the gastrointestinal tract
treatments.name: Emesis Induction (Inducing Vomiting) and Activated Charcoal
treatments.notes: This procedure is strictly indicated for asymptomatic cats following a known or suspected large ingestion of the plant. 3. Acidosis Correction and Supportive Care

treatments.description: The veterinary team will routinely monitor the cat's metabolic state using venous blood gas testing. If severe metabolic acidosis is detected, the veterinarian will correct it by administering sodium bicarbonate
treatments.name: Venous Blood Gas Monitoring and Sodium Bicarbonate
treatments.notes: While large ingestions require intensive emergency intervention, most minor exposures to cyanogenic plants in small animals only require minimal gastrointestinal supportive care if managed promptly1.
